newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Papua New Guinea to sell stake in major gold mines.
newsitem.headline: Papua New Guinea to sell stake in major gold mines.

text.p: Papua New Guinea said on Thursday it would offer investors a stake in some of the world's largest gold discoveries, confident that mine sabotage and landowner disputes in the South Pacific nation are a thing of the past.
Papua New Guinea (PNG) plans to raise about A$261 million from the Australian sharemarket listing of a 49 percent stake in Orogen Minerals Ltd, a company formed from the PNG government's mining arm.
But the PNG government is keen to keep its tribal-based voters from missing out by ensuring that 30 percent of available shares are kept at home.

Roadshows will be held over the next month to attract major fund managers in Europe, Asia, and North America, who are expected to take up 50 percent of the issue. The remainder would be acquired by small investors in Australia and New Zealand.
Orogen will hold the government's strategic investments in the giant Porgera, Lihir, and Misima gold mines as well as the Kutubu and Gobe oilfields.
The government will retain a controlling 51 percent investment in Orogen and has given the company a 25-year option to hold its sovereign share in future mining projects.
Orogen chairman David Beatty said the company would offer investors "an exposure to one of the most prospective and resource rich regions in the world".

"These assets are being developed and operated by some of the world's largest, most experienced resource companies, such as Chevron Corp, Placer Dome, and RTZ-CRA," Beatty told a news conference announcing the float and releasing a prospectus.
Orogen also had the option to include the massive Ok Tedi and Bougainville copper projects in its portfolio, he said.

But this was subject to resolution of the landowner dispute at Ok Tedi with Australian miner Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd and the end of a secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island that has closed the RTZ-CRA Panguna mine since May 1989.
"Bougainville is a problem and that is one reason why it is just put as an option," said PNG Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta.
Orogen's brokers plan to visit as many villages as possible before the November 1 listing in order to develop a wide shareholder base in PNG, a mountainous country with 700 languages and 600 islands.
Three teams, each with a translator, will go "to almost anywhere we can get an aircraft in to land", said Greg Pynt, a director at broker McIntosh Corporate, one of the lead managers.
"We are going to encourage them (villagers) to band together to buy stock. We are going to tell them what a share is all about and what it means," Pynt said.

At the request of Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan's government, Pynt said the brokers had devised an inexpensive entry package that would allow local investors to pool their funds and buy 100-share parcels at a 10 percent discount.

Even so, at a cost of K157 (US$119.32) for 100 shares, the average Papua New Guinean would appear financially stretched to invest in Orogen. The Asian Development Bank recently estimated that they have an annual income of US$750.
Wealthier shareholders in Australia and New Zealand would be offered a minimum of 2,000 Orogen shares at A$1.70 each, while the institutional price would be set under a bidding system.
